does: Fries thinly sliced onions in a generous layer of hot oil until they turn deep brown and crisp at the edges, then lifts them out to drain. They bring a bittersweet crunch to rice and lentils, and the oil they leave behind is full of their flavour.
how: Slice the onions thin and evenly, so that they brown at one pace.
Heat a good depth of oil in a wide, heavy pan until a slice sizzles the moment it goes in.
Add the onions in a loose layer, in batches if need be. Stir often at first, then less often as they darken.
Lower the heat once the edges go dark, and keep frying until the onions are a deep brown. They crisp further as they cool.
Lift them out with a slotted spoon onto a rack or paper, and salt them lightly. Keep the oil.

cues.text: A deep, even brown with a few darker tips, and no black.
A loud bubbling at the start that calms to a quiet sizzle as the water leaves the onions.
A piece lifted out and cooled snaps when it is pressed.

mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the onions steam, turn limp and never crisp.
mistakes.fix: Fry in batches, in the widest pan you have.

mistakes.mistake: Looking away at the end, when the onions go from brown to bitter black in moments.
mistakes.fix: Stay by the pan and lift them out as soon as they are deep brown.

mistakes.mistake: Starting in cool oil, which soaks into the onions and leaves them greasy.
mistakes.fix: Wait until a slice sizzles at once.

comes_after.why: Even slices brown at one pace, so a cook who can slice evenly fries better onions.

variant_of.differs: The onions are cut thin and fried in plenty of hot oil until dark and crisp at the edges, and not coaxed slowly in a little fat until soft and sweet.
